questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical CKAD skills: wiring ConfigMaps and Secrets, configuring InitContainers, implementing TLS sidecars, setting up readiness/liveness probes, and crafting a NetworkPolicy with conditional egress.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap-driven feature flags
- Secrets for credential management
- InitContainers for tooling installation
- TLS sidecars for secure communication
- Readiness and liveness probe configuration
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: feature-config
data:
  ENABLE_API: "true"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: api-creds
type: Opaque
data:
  token: <base64-encoded-token>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: app-namespace
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-policy
  namespace: app-namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: internal-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: app-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: installer
          image: curlimages/curl:latest
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'echo Initialized']
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: my-app:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: ENABLE_API
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: feature-config
                  key: ENABLE_API
            - name: API_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: api-creds
                  key: token
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /status
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /status
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
        - name: tls-sidecar
          image: nginx:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 443
```

## Trade-offs
- **NetworkPolicy complexity**: The policy above allows egress only to the internal-api pod. A more permissive approach might allow DNS resolution but restrict target services.
- **InitContainer overhead**: Installing curl in every pod increases startup time and image size. Consider baking tools into the base image if startup latency is critical.
- **Sidecar maintenance**: A TLS sidecar adds complexity and resource overhead. For simple use cases, TLS could be handled within the application container directly.
- **Secret security**: Storing credentials in a Secret is fine for basic scenarios, but consider external secrets operators or vault integration for production environments requiring rotation.
- **Probe configuration**: Aggressive probe settings can cause unnecessary restarts; conservative settings may delay failure detection. Tune based on application startup time.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests hands-on CKAD skills: in-cluster configuration, API access, and multi-resource coordination. It evaluates how the candidate wires ConfigMaps, Secrets, and PVCs into a Deployment, and how they enforce traffic restrictions with a NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts

- Namespace-scoped Deployment and RBAC permissions
- ConfigMap-based thresholds and Secret-based credentials
- API access to Namespace ResourceQuota metrics
- InitContainer usage for tools like curl/jq
- Logs persisted to a PVC mounted at /logs
- Readiness and liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy to restrict egress to the central endpoint

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: alert-config
data:
  cpu-threshold: "80"
  memory-threshold: "85"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: alert-credentials
data:
  api-key: <base64-encoded-key>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: log-storage
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: resource-watcher
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: resource-watcher
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: resource-watcher
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: installer
          image: busybox
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |-
                wget -q https://github.com/stedolan/jq/releases/download/jq-1.6/jq-linux64 -O /usr/local/bin/jq
                chmod +x /usr/local/bin/jq
                apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /usr/local/bin
      containers:
        - name: watcher
          image: your-watcher-image:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              name: http
          env:
            - name: CENTRAL_ENDPOINT
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: alert-credentials
                  key: api-key
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
              readOnly: true
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "64Mi"
              cpu: "50m"
            limits:
              memory: "128Mi"
              cpu: "100m"
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: log-storage
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: alert-config
        - name: tools
          emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-restriction
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: resource-watcher
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              name: central-monitoring
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443
```

## Trade-offs

1. **Polling vs. Watch API**: Polling ResourceQuota is simpler but adds latency; the Watch API is more efficient but requires handling event streams.
2. **Sidecar vs. Main Container**: A sidecar could handle logging while the main container focuses on monitoring—improving separation of concerns.
3. **Centralized vs. Per-Namespace**: Deploying per-namespace increases resource usage but provides isolation and reduces blast radius.
4. **PVC for Logs**: Using a PVC adds persistence but requires storage provisioning; consider sidecar streaming to stdout for easier management.
5. **InitContainer Overhead**: Downloading tools on every pod start slows startup; a custom image with tools pre-installed would be faster.

## Why This Is Asked

- NetworkPolicy basics: podSelector, ingress/egress, policyTypes

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical batch-job composition: init tooling, config-driven scripts, and safe cleanup. 

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes Job TTL, backoff, and completion semantics
- InitContainers alongside main containers
- ConfigMap and Secret mounts; env from Secret
- Resource requests/limits; idempotence

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migrate
  namespace: migrate
spec:
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 600
  backoffLimit: 3
  completions: 1
  parallelism: 1
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache postgresql-client"]
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: postgres:15
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: db-creds
          env:
            - name: PGHOST
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-creds
                  key: host
          command: ["psql","-h","$(PGHOST)","-U","$(POSTGRES_USER)","-d","migration_db","-f","/migrate/scripts/migrate.sql"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: migrate-scripts
              mountPath: /migrate/scripts
      volumes:
        - name: migrate-scripts
          configMap:
            name: migrate-scripts
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate idempotence for repeated runs?
- How would you rollback if migration fails after partial progress?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question validates understanding of per-namespace resource governance in Kubernetes. It tests knowledge of how LimitRange and ResourceQuota work together to control pod sizing and cluster resource allocation.

## Key Concepts
- **LimitRange**: Sets default requests/limits applied to Pods that don't specify resources
- **ResourceQuota**: Enforces hard limits on total namespace resource consumption
- **Policy alignment**: Ensuring Deployments specify resources matching namespace defaults
- **Verification**: Testing policy enforcement with intentional over-allocation
- **Rollback**: Strategy for removing or scaling back resources when policies need adjustment

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: analytics-lr
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:
      cpu: "200m"
      memory: 256Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: 128Mi
```
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: analytics-quo
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  hard:
    cpu: "400m"
    memory: 512Mi
    requests.storage: "1Gi"
```
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: reporter
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: reporter
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
```
## Verification Commands
```bash
kubectl apply -f limitrange.yaml
kubectl apply -f quota.yaml
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl describe resourcequota analytics-quo -n analytics
kubectl run overload-test --image=busybox --restart=Never --requests=cpu=500m,memory=600Mi --dry-run=server
```
## Rollback Strategy
```bash
kubectl delete -f quota.yaml
kubectl delete -f limitrange.yaml
kubectl scale deployment reporter --replicas=0 -n analytics
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to compose common CKAD primitives into a cohesive, maintainable per-namespace app: InitContainer logic, ConfigMap-driven behavior, TLS handling, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer installs rendering tool and pre-processes inputs
- ConfigMap and Secret drive runtime config and secrets
- Sidecar for TLS rotation and secret refresh
- Readiness/Liveness probes for quick failure detection
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricts egress to internal endpoints

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: docs-portal
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: docs-portal
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: docs-portal
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: docs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: docs-pvc
        - name: tls-cert
          secret:
            secretName: docs-tls
      initContainers:
        - name: render-md
          image: pandoc/pandoc:latest
          command: ["sh", "-c", "cp -r /docs/* /rendered/; pandoc -f markdown -t html /docs/*.md -o /rendered/index.html"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: docs
              mountPath: /docs
            - name: rendered
              mountPath: /rendered
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:stable
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: rendered
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses familiarity with ConfigMap mounts, InitContainers, and sidecar reload patterns within a single namespace. It also evaluates understanding of signal-based versus in-process reload mechanisms, along with basic security practices using Secrets and NetworkPolicies.

## Key Concepts
- **ConfigMap-driven runtime config**: Externalizing configuration allows updates without rebuilding containers
- **InitContainer provisioning**: Installing tooling (inotify-tools) needed by sidecars or main containers
- **Sidecar watching**: File change detection using inotifywait triggers graceful reloads without container restart
- **Signal-based reloads**: SIGHUP triggers graceful reloads; alternative approaches include local /reload API endpoints
- **Security with Secrets**: Sensitive data like admin credentials should mount via Secrets, not environment variables
- **NetworkPolicy**: Namespace-level egress restrictions limit exposure of internal endpoints

## Trade-offs
- **Signal vs. API reload**: SIGHUP requires the application to handle signals gracefully; /reload APIs add complexity but offer finer control
- **inotifywait vs. polling**: inotifywait is event-driven and efficient but limited to the container filesystem; polling works cross-platform but incurs overhead
- **Sidecar vs. embedded reload**: Sidecars keep concerns separated but add resource overhead; embedding reload logic reduces complexity but couples concerns
- **ConfigMap vs. volume plugins**: Native ConfigMap mounts require pod recreation for updates; external volume plugins enable dynamic updates at the cost of complexity

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests basic CKAD concepts: PVC-backed watches, policy-driven validation, InitContainers, Secrets, sidecars, network policies, and external API reporting.

## Key Concepts

- Deployment, PVC, ConfigMap, Secret
- YAML validation with yq/jq; policy-driven checks
- InitContainer and TLS-sidecar patterns
- NetworkPolicy egress controls; readiness/liveness probes

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal skeleton: policy-watcher Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: policy-watcher
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
      - name: pods-pvc
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: pods-pvc
      - name: policies
        configMap:
          name: policy-config
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.19
        command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache yq jq"]
      containers:
      - name: watcher
        image: <registry>/policy-watcher:latest
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: api-creds
        volumeMounts:
        - name: pods-pvc
          mountPath: /pods
        - name: policies
          mountPath: /policies
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test this in CI for policy regressions?
- What happens when policy-config changes at runtime?
